finding: §2 asserts that 'under `tp run` the §6.2 fence already denies the write, so the constraint is enforced and this text is a courtesy'. Verified against the shipped mechanism: spec/0.35.0.md §6.2 line 471 and skills/tp/REFERENCE.md line 395 scope the PreToolUse deny to `.tp-review/` contents, `*.tasks.json`, `.tp/config.json` and `.tp/local.json` only, and lines 479-483 state 'Shell tools are deliberately outside the matcher: the denial exists to stop hand-editing, not to sandbox.' The mutation §2 describes -- an auditor editing a repository SOURCE file to test a tautological test -- is denied by neither the path list nor the tool matcher, and a shell redirect is not matched at all. So the unattended path is exactly as unprotected as the interactive one. Two scoping decisions rest on this false premise (§2's 'This release covers the second case only' and Non-Goal 4's 'The interactive path gets the instruction, not a fence'), and an implementer building to them ships a release whose notes claim unattended runs are fenced when they are not.
suggestion: Re-derive the claim against spec/0.35.0.md §6.2 and rewrite §2's last paragraph: under `tp run` the emitted text is the ONLY protection too, because the fence covers tp state files and not repo sources. Then either (a) state plainly that the constraint is instruction-only on both paths and drop the courtesy/enforced distinction from §2 and Non-Goal 4, or (b) if enforcement under `tp run` is actually wanted, say so as an explicit requirement (extend the matcher / add a source-write deny) with its own test -- but do not leave the release resting on a fence that does not exist.

finding: §2 states as fact that 'under `tp run` the §6.2 fence already denies the write, so the constraint is enforced and this text is a courtesy'. Checked against the cited section: `spec/0.35.0.md` §6.2's `PreToolUse` denial covers exactly `.tp-review/` contents, `*.tasks.json`, `.tp/config.json` and `.tp/local.json` — tp's own state files — and that section says in as many words that 'Shell tools are deliberately outside the matcher: the denial exists to stop hand-editing, not to sandbox.' The §2 scenario is an auditor mutating a repository SOURCE file, which that fence does not deny by any tool and does not deny at all via Bash. So the premise is false, and it is the premise §5 non-goal 4 rests on ('The interactive path gets the instruction, not a fence') — the scoping argument concludes the unattended path is already protected when it is not. No §6 test asserts the claim, so nothing would catch it.
suggestion: Either correct §2 to say the fence does not cover source files under `tp run` either (making the emitted clause the only protection on both paths, and non-goal 4's asymmetry unnecessary), or extend `spec/0.35.0.md` §6.2's matcher and cite the extension. Whichever is chosen, add a §6 test that pins the actual denial set rather than leaving the claim untested.

finding: Incremental append silently destroys the only signal `tp run` has for "this role finished". spec/0.35.0.md §3.3 defines the durable write of `review-role` and `audit-role` as "`$TP_ROUND_DIR/role-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson` exists and every line parses", and §6.2's Stop hook applies that same predicate — "present and wholly parseable" — to the `.part` file. That predicate is a completeness proxy that works only because a buffering unit writes the file once, as its last act. Under §3's mechanism the file exists and parses from the moment row 1 is appended. Consequences, all silent: (a) the Stop hook can no longer block a role that stops with 3 of 40 items judged — the very guard that today makes a short round continue; (b) §3.3.1's success test ("exited 0 AND its durable write is present") is satisfied by that unit, so the driver renames `.part` to the final name and the round merges a 3-row role as a complete one; (c) spec/0.35.0.md §10.6 test 52 asserts hook, oracle and driver agree — after this change they agree on the wrong answer. This re-opens spec/0.35.0.md §8a.4 ("A dropped role does not merge clean") in a new form, and §3's own argument is what makes it undetectable: "a findings file is append-only NDJSON whose partial state is already valid input to `--merge`" is exactly why nothing downstream can tell partial from complete. The crash path stays protected, because a crashed child exits non-zero and is never renamed; the exposed case is the clean early stop — an agent that believes it is done, or that returns normally at a context or turn limit.
suggestion: This release must supply a completeness marker that a partial file lacks, and say which component reads it. The cheapest shape consistent with the existing design: the unit appends a terminal sentinel row (or writes a sibling `role-<id>.done`) as its last act, and §3.3's predicate becomes "parseable AND terminated" — a one-line change to a predicate spec/0.35.0.md deliberately kept to two conditions so a hook can evaluate it. Whatever the shape, it belongs in this spec, not in spec/0.41.0.md or spec/0.42.0.md: this release is what invalidates the current predicate, so the repair is not another spec's to own.

finding: Tests 1 and 2 assert the presence of emitted text ('contains the working-tree constraint and the copy-out recipe', 'instructs incremental append, and states the reason') but no §6-checkable form of that text exists anywhere in the spec. §2 and §3 give the intent in prose; neither gives a literal string, a stable substring, or a required keyword set. A grep-based test therefore greps for whatever token the implementer happened to write, which is the tautology shape this project's evidence rule names: the assertion is derived from the implementation, so it cannot fail against it. It also silently passes for a prompt whose clause is present but semantically wrong (e.g. carries the prohibition but omits the copy-out recipe, which is the half that makes the constraint livable).
suggestion: Add an appendix pinning the two clauses verbatim (or a required substring per clause), and restate tests 1 and 2 as literal-substring assertions against that appendix. Separately assert the three distinguishable parts of clause 1 — may read anything / must not modify / copy out before mutating — so a partial implementation fails.

finding: The channel argument for emitting the isolation clause rules out only skills/tp/SKILL.md. It never prices the channel that already exists and already carries this exact rule: the plugin ships agents/tp-reviewer.md and agents/tp-auditor.md, and both already say 'You may write exactly one file ... Every other write is refused - another role's file, another round, the merged file, the spec, the source.' That definition IS handed to the same fresh process the spec appeals to, and it is loaded once per unit rather than once per role per round. Emitting the same substance again costs roles x rounds x phases (4 x ~10 x 2 = ~80 prompt copies per cycle on this repo alone) to deliver text that arrives free on every runtime that loads the definitions. The only part genuinely absent from the definitions is the copy-out recipe, which could be added there for the same zero marginal cost.
suggestion: Add a paragraph to §2 that names agents/tp-reviewer.md and agents/tp-auditor.md as the competing channel and states why they are insufficient — e.g. tp is runtime-agnostic and a non-Claude-Code driver loads no agent definition. If that is the real argument, say it; then scope the emitted clause to the case the definitions cannot cover, and put the copy-out recipe in the definitions where it is paid for once.

finding: The copy-out recipe does not support the experiment class §2's own motivating story describes, so it is not "the recipe that makes the constraint livable". The field instance is an auditor that "mutated a file in the repository to test whether a test was tautological", and the collision was a concurrent auditor running the static analyser. Copying one file out of the repository and mutating the copy does not let you run that repository's test suite or static analyser against the mutation — a Go file outside its module, a PHP class outside its autoloader, are not runnable subjects. The experiment the project's own evidence rule demands (CLAUDE.md: "inject the failure the code claims to catch"; spec/0.42.0.md §3: "The informative experiment is the one that could have failed") requires the mutation to be in a tree the tooling can be pointed at. The spec therefore replaces a working-but-unsafe practice with a safe one that cannot do the job, and no section notices.
suggestion: Say what the copied-out subject is: a whole scratch clone/worktree of the repository (the shape CLAUDE.md already uses for gremlins — "Run it in an rsync copy, never the repo"), not a copied file. If a whole-tree copy is out of scope for this release, then the honest text is "restore the mutation byte-identically before yielding, and do not run a mutation concurrently with other roles" — and the concurrency consequence of that must be stated, because spec/0.42.0.md §9 records that role units are run concurrently precisely on the premise that they are read-only.

finding: The copy-out recipe is emitted as the thing that makes the constraint livable, and §2 defers the execution-surface question to spec/0.42.0.md §9 — but §9 has already assessed this exact recipe and found against it: 'N auditors each building a scratch copy would dissolve the concurrency argument', and 'Any design owes an execution surface — a per-unit workspace in the child environment and an amended agent definition — or must say plainly that perturbation is interactive-only.' So this release ships the mechanism the deferred section names as the problem, and prices neither half of it. Cost one: a scratch copy per auditor per round is real wall-clock, disk and tool-call spend that scales with panel size, and §9 says it costs the concurrency argument too. Cost two is worse — for the experiment class §2 itself cites (mutate a file to check whether a test or a static analyser is tautological) a copy taken OUT of the repository is not runnable by the project toolchain: a Go file outside its package does not compile, golangci-lint and go test operate on the project rather than a stray file, and a PHP class outside its autoload root is never loaded. The unit therefore spends discovery round-trips on a recipe that cannot produce the observation, then either abandons the experiment or mutates in place — which is exactly what §2's own evidence records ('one auditor still had to be told separately to restore a mutation byte-identically').
suggestion: Say what 0.42.0 §9 says a design owes. Under tp run, state that perturbation is unavailable and the emitted text is a prohibition with no recipe attached (dropping the recipe's bytes on the path where it cannot be used). On the interactive path, name the form that is actually runnable — a copy of the repository, which CLAUDE.md already prescribes for gremlins runs ('Run it in an rsync copy, never the repo') — rather than 'copies the subject out of the repository', and state its per-unit cost so the trade is visible.

finding: The entire deliverable of §2 and §3 is prompt WORDING, and neither section gives the wording. §2 describes the constraint in prose ('a unit may read anything, must not modify the working tree, and when an experiment needs a mutation it copies the subject out of the repository first and mutates the copy') and §3 says the prompt 'instructs the unit to write each row as it is decided ... and says why in one clause' -- but no normative string is fixed anywhere. I cannot write the commit: I would invent two paragraphs, and test 1 ('contains the working-tree constraint and the copy-out recipe') has no fixture to assert against, so it degrades into a keyword search whose keywords I also invent. This is the failure class CLAUDE.md names for auditor evidence, reproduced in a test.
suggestion: Put the exact emitted text in the spec, verbatim, in a fenced block for each clause -- as the normative artifact, with the implementation reduced to a named constant (e.g. `engine.IsolationClause`, `engine.IncrementalWriteClause`). Then tests 1 and 2 assert prompt-contains-constant and a separate test asserts the constant equals the spec block, which is what makes the assertion refutable.

finding: The mechanism prescribes a recipe — "when an experiment needs a mutation it copies the subject out of the repository first and mutates the copy" — that a unit running under `tp run` cannot execute. spec/0.35.0.md §6.3 states the reviewer and auditor "may write exactly one path" (their findings `.part` file, plus the escalation record) "and are denied every other write". Copying a file out of the repository is a write to a second path. So the emitted prompt, which §2 gives no path-conditional variant, instructs every fenced audit unit to perform an action its own agent definition forbids; the unit either burns attempts on denied writes or silently abandons the experiment. spec/0.42.0.md §9 names this exact hole — "Perturbation has nowhere to happen" — and asks any design to supply a per-unit workspace "or must say plainly that perturbation is interactive-only". This spec does neither: it ships the recipe unconditionally and defers the surface.
suggestion: Either (a) state that the copy-out clause is emitted only when `TP_ROUND_DIR` is unset — i.e. the recipe is interactive-only — and say so in the prompt text itself so a fenced unit is not told to do the impossible, or (b) name the one writable scratch path a fenced unit may use and add it to §6.3's allowlist as a task in this release. Option (b) decides part of spec/0.42.0.md §9 and must be recorded there.

finding: §2 concedes the clause is inert on the primary path: 'under tp run the §6.2 fence already denies the write, so the constraint is enforced and this text is a courtesy'. Verified against source — hooks/pre-tool-use-role-write-allow.sh is a deny-by-default allowlist that refuses any write outside the unit's own findings file. Yet the Mechanism paragraph emits the clause unconditionally, so under tp run (which CLAUDE.md now names the PRIMARY self-development model) every role prompt of every round carries bytes that feed no decision the agent can act on differently. A courtesy that costs ~80 prompt copies per cycle is not a courtesy, it is the definition of an unearned byte.
suggestion: Decide and state the gating. tp already knows it is running under a driver (TP_UNATTENDED / TP_ROUND_DIR are in the child environment), so emit the isolation clause only when the fence is absent — or, if unconditional emission is preferred for simplicity, say so explicitly and state the accepted cost rather than leaving 'courtesy' as the last word on it.

finding: §2 justifies the whole interactive/run split with "under `tp run` the §6.2 fence already denies the write". That is the wrong section and the wrong fence. spec/0.35.0.md §6.2's PreToolUse denial covers exactly four targets — `.tp-review/` contents, `*.tasks.json`, `.tp/config.json`, `.tp/local.json` — and no repository source file, so it would not have denied the PHP cycle's mutation of a source file for one instant. The thing that actually denies a source write under a run is §6.3's `tp-auditor` agent definition (spec/0.42.0.md §9 cites §6.3 correctly, so the two specs disagree on which mechanism holds). §6.3 then says of itself: "A runner that cannot load a plugin gets no agent definitions, and the unit runs without them. The restrictions are defence in depth" — and the `--agent` flag is appended only by the `claude` runner template. So under `tp run` with any other runner, or with a plugin that failed to load, nothing denies the write either, and this text is not a courtesy there — it is the only thing standing.
suggestion: Correct the citation to §6.3, and rewrite the split on what is actually true: the emitted constraint is the primary mechanism on the interactive path AND on any run whose runner or plugin does not supply the agent definition; §6.3's restriction is a second layer that exists only for the `claude` runner with the plugin loaded. Drop the word "courtesy" — it licenses treating the run path as covered when §6.3 explicitly declines to be a durable contract.

finding: §2's constraint is 'a unit may read anything, must not modify the working tree', but §3 requires the same unit to append each finding row to its NDJSON file as it is decided — and that file lives in the working tree (verified: v0.35.1 emits `output_path` values like `review-r1-tester.ndjson`, repo-relative). Taken literally the emitted prompt tells the unit both to not write to the working tree and to write to the working tree. §2 also quotes two different scopes for the same rule without reconciling them: the field operator's 'DO NOT modify the working tree' and tp's own 'Do NOT modify any repo source file' — the second permits the findings write, the first forbids it. A test for test 1 cannot decide which text is correct, and a unit that reads the stricter clause will refuse to produce output at all.
suggestion: Pin one scope and carve out the exception explicitly, e.g. 'do not modify any file the repository tracks, except your own findings file at <output_path>'. State that scope once in §2 and let §6 test 1 assert the carve-out is present, not just the prohibition.

finding: Incremental append is the single largest agent-side cost in this release and the spec never prices it. It converts one write per unit into one write per finding: §3's own evidence cites a 72-row round, i.e. 71 extra tool round-trips for that unit, and the Mechanism explicitly instructs the agent NOT to batch them back ('so an agent that is optimising its own tool calls does not batch the writes back together'). Tool-call round-trips are exactly the currency P1 and P3 defend, and this spends them deliberately and without a bound. §1's claim that the release 'changes nothing about what a round asks' is inaccurate on this axis — it does not change the checklist, but it materially changes the unit's tool-call budget.
suggestion: State the trade in §3: durability is bought with N-1 extra writes per unit, and say why that is the right price (a lost round costs a full re-run; a write costs one round-trip). If a bound is acceptable, express it — 'never hold more than one decided finding unwritten' is a rule an agent can follow and a test can check; 'write incrementally' is not. And soften §1 to 'changes nothing about what a round asks or how convergence is counted' only if the tool-call change is acknowledged elsewhere.

finding: 'writes one file per role, named from the role' (§4) and 'each name derives from its role' (test 3) never fix the naming scheme: no extension (.md? .txt? .prompt.md? .json?), no round or phase component, and no statement of whether review and audit writing into the same --out-dir collide (both panels can contain a role of the same name; `tp review`'s own output_path already disambiguates with a `review-r<N>-` prefix). Worse, role names are user-authored: this repo's panel comes from `.tp/reviewers/*.json` and `.tp/auditors/*.json`, so a role name containing `/`, `..`, a leading `-`, or a NUL is caller-supplied data flowing straight into a write path -- the exact sink-guard case CLAUDE.md calls out for SafeGitRev. The spec gives me neither the format nor the guard.
suggestion: Fix the scheme literally, e.g. `<out-dir>/<phase>-r<round>-<role>.prompt.md`, and state the sanitisation rule at the sink: a role name that is not `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]*` is refused with a hint naming the role and the file is not written (or the name is slugified -- but say which). Add a test for a hostile role name.

finding: --out-dir is specified against exactly one of the command's modes (--merge, test 8) while `tp review` has seven others that reach different code paths and emit different payloads: --record, --status, --report, --verify, --resolve/--resolve-all, --diff-from, and --perspective documentation|testing|code-audit (verified in `tp review --help`, which groups --merge/--resolve/--verify/--report as 'Modes (mutually exclusive)'); `tp audit` has its own set. For every one of them I have to invent whether --out-dir is accepted, ignored, or refused, and the modes are not symmetric -- --verify and --perspective DO emit a prompt (so --out-dir is arguably meaningful), while --status and --report emit no prompt at all.
suggestion: Add one sentence enumerating acceptance: --out-dir is valid only in prompt-emitting invocations (default panel emission, and explicitly say yes/no for --verify and --perspective); with every non-emitting mode it exits 2 with a hint naming the conflicting mode. One row per mode in a small table is cheaper than eight rounds of re-litigation.

finding: With --out-dir the prompt bodies are emitted twice. Measured on this very round, the four role prompts are 3941-4094 bytes each (~16 KB for a 4-role panel, ~20 KB for the 5-role field panel) — the largest single thing tp emits. §4 says only that the flag 'writes one file per role' and 'reports the paths on the machine-readable surface'; nothing removes prompts[].prompt from stdout. A caller that asked for files has, by that act, said it does not want the bodies inline, so the flag as specified doubles the payload precisely for the caller who least needs it. Test 7 is the only payload-shape test and it constrains the WITHOUT-flag case, so nothing in §6 can catch the doubling.
suggestion: Specify the with-flag payload: under --out-dir, prompts[] carries role, output_path and the written prompt-file path, and the prompt body is omitted (or retained only under an explicit opt-in). Add a test that the --out-dir payload is strictly smaller than the default one and contains no prompt body.

finding: §4 says the flag 'is additive: without the flag the emitted JSON is unchanged' but never says what the payload looks like WITH the flag. The load-bearing question is whether `prompts[].prompt` (the large prompt body) is still inlined on stdout when it has also been written to a file. Both readings are consistent with the spec text: (a) prompts are still inlined and the files are a duplicate copy, (b) the bodies are elided and only the paths remain. Verified against v0.35.1: `tp review <spec>` emits four `prompts[]` objects each carrying the full `prompt` string, so the difference between (a) and (b) is the entire token saving the release is arguing for. Two engineers write contradictory tests for test 7 and test 5 depending on which they assume.
suggestion: State explicitly in §4 whether `prompts[].prompt` is retained, elided, or elided only under `--compact`, when `--out-dir` is given, and add a §6 test asserting the chosen shape.

finding: §4 says the flag 'reports the paths on the machine-readable surface' and test 5 says 'the written paths appear on the machine-readable surface' -- but the field is never named or shaped, and the payload it lands in already has a confusable key. Verified today: `tp review <spec> --json` emits `prompts[]` with keys role, category, prompt, output_path, where output_path is the FINDINGS destination (`review-r1-implementer.ndjson`), not a prompt file. A second per-role path with no name is the one thing a driver must parse, and if it reuses or shadows `output_path` every existing consumer silently spawns against the wrong file. The spec also never says whether `prompts[].prompt` remains in the payload when --out-dir is given (duplicating the whole prompt body next to its own file) or is replaced by the path.
suggestion: Name the field and its shape explicitly, e.g. `prompts[].prompt_path` (absolute or cwd-relative -- say which), and state that `output_path` keeps its current findings meaning unchanged. Decide and state whether `prompts[].prompt` stays, is emptied, or is omitted under --out-dir, since that is the difference between a payload a driver can stream and one that doubles in size.

finding: Non-Goal 2 defers "deciding the auditor's execution surface" to spec/0.42.0.md §9 while §2's mechanism decides half of it. §2 of that file lists what is deferred as "a per-unit workspace, an amended agent definition, a sanctioned way to perturb" — and §2's own mechanism then ships a sanctioned way to perturb ("copies the subject out of the repository first and mutates the copy") as emitted, normative prompt text. spec/0.42.0.md §9 closes with the disjunction this release is answering half of: any design "owes an execution surface … or must say plainly that perturbation is interactive-only". This spec takes neither branch cleanly: it prescribes the recipe unconditionally, says it "covers the second case only", and leaves the question open in the other file. The result is a genuinely unowned gap — what an auditor does under `tp run` when the evidence rule (spec/0.42.0.md §3, CLAUDE.md) requires a perturbation it is fenced from performing is claimed by neither file, because this one excludes it and that one calls it open.
suggestion: Pick a branch and record it in both files. Either this release states plainly that perturbation is interactive-only — which is one of the two answers spec/0.42.0.md §9 explicitly asks for, and would let §9 close half its question — or the recipe is withdrawn from §2 until §9 decides, leaving §2 with the constraint alone. Shipping the recipe while disclaiming ownership of it is the seam.

finding: Non-Goal 3 asserts "no convergence arithmetic changes. Convergence is spec/0.37.0.md", and §1 repeats it ("It changes nothing about what a round asks or how convergence is counted"). §3's mechanism falsifies that. Convergence is counted from the merged round; what enters the merge is each role's findings file; what admits a role's file is spec/0.35.0.md §3.3's "exists and every line parses" predicate — which incremental append satisfies after the first row. So this release changes which role outputs are admitted as complete, and therefore what every convergence count is computed over, without changing a single line of arithmetic. That is not spec/0.37.0.md's problem to fix: that file owns the counting rule (`audit_converge_on`, dispositions, spec-hash resets) and takes the round's row set as given. The input side is this release's.
suggestion: Withdraw the unconditional claim and replace it with the precise one: no counting rule changes, but the admission predicate for a role's findings file does, and this release owns the repair. Then state the repaired predicate here (see the §3 finding) so spec/0.37.0.md's replay test against the nine recorded v0.35.0 audit rounds is still computing over the same population it was designed for.

finding: Test 7 requires the emitted JSON to be 'byte-identical to the current output', but names no baseline artifact. 'The current output' is not a fixture: it is whatever the binary at some unstated ref prints, for an unstated spec, with unstated flags and unstated review state. One engineer diffs against a checked-in golden file, another against a v0.35.1 binary built from a stash, a third writes nothing because there is nothing to compare to. The assertion is also state-sensitive — the payload carries `review_loop` and `skipped_roles`, which vary with recorded rounds and the role corpus.
suggestion: Pin the baseline: name a golden fixture committed with the release (e.g. a recorded payload for a fixture spec under a fixed corpus with `--no-state`), and state the exact flag set the comparison runs under.

finding: Test 7's 'byte-identical ... apart from the two new prompt clauses' is not a mechanically checkable assertion. A byte comparison admits no 'apart from' unless both the exact clause text and its exact insertion point are pinned, and the spec pins neither — §2 and §3 describe the clauses only in prose ('carries the constraint and the recipe', 'instructs the unit to write each row as it is decided ... and says why in one clause'). Without pinned text the test degrades into a human eyeball diff, which is exactly the class of check that passes whatever the implementation did.
suggestion: Either (a) pin the two clauses verbatim in an appendix and make test 7 assert `baseline == actual with the two literal clauses removed`, or (b) drop 'byte-identical' and assert the checkable property instead: every top-level key, every `prompts[]` key, the role set, and the `output_path` values are unchanged, and the only differing bytes are inside `prompts[].prompt`.

finding: Test 8 asserts a disjunction: `--out-dir` and `--merge`'s `--output` 'do not collide: passing both is either coherent or refused with a hint, never silently one-of'. A test cannot assert a disjunction — it must assert one branch. As written, an implementation that accepts both and an implementation that rejects both both pass, which means the test discriminates nothing. It also rests on an unverified premise: in v0.35.1, `-o/--output` without `--merge` already exits 2 with the hint 'tp review writes its payload to stdout; redirect it, or use --merge to write an NDJSON file with -o', so the two flags can only meet inside `--merge` mode — and the spec never says whether `--out-dir` is legal in `--merge` mode at all.
suggestion: Choose the branch. Recommended: `--out-dir` is an emit-mode flag, so passing it with `--merge` (or `--record`/`--status`/`--resolve`/`--report`/`--verify`) exits 2 with a hint naming the mode — mirroring the existing `--output requires --merge` guard. Then test 8 becomes a single deterministic assertion with a pinned exit code.

finding: Test 8 says passing --out-dir with --merge's --output 'is either coherent or refused with a hint, never silently one-of'. That is not a contract -- it is the spec handing the implementer the decision and then asserting whichever branch I pick, so the test passes under two opposite behaviours and no reviewer of the resulting code can say it is wrong. Precedent already exists and the spec does not use it: `tp review --merge partial.ndjson --no-state` today exits 2 with `{"error":"--merge cannot be combined with --harness-note/--force/--no-state/--perspective/--docs-path/--test-path","code":2,"hint":"run --merge on its own..."}`, i.e. --merge already refuses incompatible flags with a specific exit code and hint.
suggestion: Decide it in the spec: --out-dir is an emit-mode flag, so combining it with --merge exits 2 and extends the existing 'cannot be combined with' error list and hint. Then test 8 asserts one behaviour: exit 2, message names both flags.

finding: The release's entire mechanism is adding bytes to every emitted prompt, and the spec contains no cost accounting of any kind: no byte budget for the two clauses, no cap on their length, no statement of the per-cycle multiplier, and no test bounding them. P3 says every output byte costs agent context, which makes that accounting this spec's own obligation rather than a nicety. The measured baseline is available — role prompts on this repo are ~4 KB, so a 500-byte pair of clauses is a ~12% increase applied to roles x rounds x phases — and the spec cites round and role counts for both cycles already, so the arithmetic is one sentence away.
suggestion: Add a short cost paragraph to §1 stating the baseline prompt size, the added clause budget, and the per-cycle total, with the argument for why that is less than the operator cost it removes. That is the trade the spec is actually making and right now it is the only trade the spec does not state.

finding: §1's claim to be "the smallest thing in the queue and deliberately first" is contradicted by the repository's own ordering record. CLAUDE.md's "Where the next work is" names v0.36.0 as "what the loop costs — makes the two largest review-loop costs visible" with a §8 release gate about suppression, v0.37.0 as the release that turns process rules into checks, and v0.38.0 as the evidence contract. The files on disk say otherwise: v0.36.0 is this spec, "what the loop costs" is now spec/0.40.0.md (whose §8 is the suppression gate CLAUDE.md describes and which spec/0.41.0.md §6 cites), "the rules become checks" is spec/0.39.0.md, the evidence contract is spec/0.42.0.md, and spec/0.38.0.md is "The backlog release". The queue was renumbered and the document that tells a fresh unit which spec to open was not, so a unit briefed from CLAUDE.md opens this file expecting suppression mechanisms and finds none.
suggestion: The repair is probably CLAUDE.md's rather than this spec's, but this release is the one that makes the drift load-bearing, so it should carry it: add the queue update to this version's scope (it is the release that occupies the renumbered slot), or drop §1's "deliberately first" claim so the spec stops asserting an ordering no committed document records.

finding: 'the §6.2 fence' carries no document qualifier, while the sentence immediately before it qualifies its reference fully (`spec/0.42.0.md` §9). Resolved inside this document, §6 is 'Tests' — a flat eight-item list with no §6.2 subsection — so a local reading lands on test item 2, the incremental-append test, which is not a fence. The intended target is `spec/0.35.0.md` §6.2. A reader or a lint rule cannot resolve it deterministically.
suggestion: Write 'spec/0.35.0.md §6.2', matching the qualification style used for the §9 reference in the same paragraph.

finding: 'under tp run the §6.2 fence already denies the write' cites the wrong subsection, and the citation is unqualified in a document that has its own §6. Verified: spec/0.35.0.md §6.2 Hooks denies writes to .tp-review/ contents, *.tasks.json, .tp/config.json and .tp/local.json — none of which is a repo source file, so §6.2 does NOT deny the mutation §2 describes. The denial comes from §6.3 Agents, the deny-by-default allowlist implemented in hooks/pre-tool-use-role-write-allow.sh. The conclusion survives, the citation does not, and resolving it costs a reader a full cross-document round-trip.
suggestion: Write it as 'spec/0.35.0.md §6.3's write allowlist' — naming the document as the neighbouring 0.41.0/0.42.0 references already do, and naming the subsection that actually holds the rule.

finding: §2 at least argues its channel (rejecting SKILL.md); §3 makes no channel argument at all — it states 'The emitted prompt instructs the unit to write each row as it is decided' as if per-prompt were the only option. Yet the incremental-write rule is the most invariant text in the whole release: it does not vary by role, by round, by phase or by spec. Fully invariant text repeated once per role per round is the textbook case for a once-per-unit channel, and agents/tp-reviewer.md and agents/tp-auditor.md already name that unit's one writable file, which is the natural place to say how to write it.
suggestion: Either move the incremental-append instruction into the two agent definitions (where it is delivered once and already sits beside the sentence naming the findings file), or give §3 the same explicit channel argument §2 has, so the per-round cost is a stated choice rather than an unexamined default.

finding: --compact is a global flag on review and audit ('minimal JSON: omit descriptions, source_lines, metadata') and the spec never mentions it. Two new things need a compact answer and get none: whether the two prompt clauses are strippable under --compact, and what --compact --out-dir emits. The second is the sharpest case — a caller who asks for both has said twice over that it wants the smallest possible payload, and it is exactly the combination where the prompt bodies should not appear on stdout.
suggestion: Add a sentence stating the --compact behaviour for both additions: the clauses are part of the prompt body and therefore not compact-strippable (they are instructions the unit must obey, not metadata), and --compact --out-dir emits paths only. Add a test pinning the --compact --out-dir payload.

finding: --out-dir is the third destination concept on the same two commands and the spec relates it to only one of them. §4 distinguishes it from --output; it never mentions TP_ROUND_DIR, which spec/0.35.0.md §6.3 already establishes as the per-round directory seam that review and audit read to emit each role's findings path. An agent now has to hold three rules: TP_ROUND_DIR says where a role's findings go, --output names a merged file, --out-dir names where prompts land. Knob economy is a real AX cost and the spec does not argue why the existing directory seam could not carry this too.
suggestion: Add one sentence to §4 stating the relation to TP_ROUND_DIR — either why prompts must not go where findings go, or that --out-dir defaults to TP_ROUND_DIR when set. Extend test 8's non-collision requirement to cover the TP_ROUND_DIR/--out-dir pair as well as --output.

finding: Moving the prompt into a file changes where its relative paths resolve, and the spec does not address it. Verified today: `prompts[].output_path` is cwd-relative (`review-r1-implementer.ndjson`), and the emitted prompt body also carries relative references -- the round's findings filename ('Write this round's findings to: review-r1-implementer.ndjson') and the spec path. Once the prompt lives in <out-dir> a driver may reasonably spawn the unit with cwd=<out-dir>, and the unit then writes its NDJSON where --merge and --record are not looking. This is the failure mode the flag is supposed to remove, reintroduced one layer down.
suggestion: State the anchor: paths inside an --out-dir-written prompt are relative to the invocation's cwd (not the out-dir), or are absolutised when --out-dir is used. Pick one and add it to test 5, which currently only checks that paths appear, not that they resolve.

finding: The whole point of this flag is a loop that runs it once per round, yet §4 never says what happens when --out-dir points at a directory that already has last round's files. Three behaviours are all defensible and observably different: silently overwrite, refuse a non-empty directory, or scope by round (r1/, r2/). Overwrite is not benign here -- the panel is not fixed between rounds (the emitted payload carries `skipped_roles`, and per-spec role activation shipped in v0.32.0), so a round with a smaller panel leaves a STALE prompt file from the previous round beside the fresh ones, with nothing distinguishing them. A driver that spawns from the directory listing then runs a dropped role's old prompt -- which is the 'a dropped role merges clean' hazard spec/0.35.0.md §8a already names.
suggestion: Decide and state it: either the file name carries the round (see the naming finding) so rounds cannot collide, or --out-dir removes only files it is about to rewrite and the spec says stale files are the driver's problem. Whichever, add a test for two consecutive rounds with different panel sizes into one directory.

finding: `--out-dir` introduces a second per-role file namespace without saying how it relates to the one that already exists. Today each emitted prompt object carries `output_path` — verified on v0.35.1: `review-r1-architect.ndjson` etc., a bare relative filename with no directory, resolved against the unit's cwd; under `tp run`, spec/0.35.0.md §6.3 rebases it to `$TP_ROUND_DIR/role-<id>.ndjson.part` via an environment variable. `--out-dir` now sets a directory for a different artifact (the prompt) through a third mechanism (a flag). The spec never says whether `--out-dir` also rebases `output_path`, so a driver that "spawns from them without parsing prose" (§4) reads prompts from `<dir>/` while its children write findings into whatever cwd they inherit — the split the flag exists to remove. §4 also says the written paths go "on the machine-readable surface" without naming the field, and the obvious name collides with the existing `output_path`, which points the other way (findings out, not prompt in).
suggestion: State the field name explicitly (e.g. `prompt_path`, distinct from `output_path`) and decide the rebasing question in one sentence: either `--out-dir` sets only the prompt destination and `output_path` is untouched, or it rebases both. Also state the overwrite policy across rounds — `output_path` carries the round number (`review-r1-...`) while §4's naming rule is "named from the role" only, so a driver reusing one directory overwrites the previous round's prompts with no diagnostic.

finding: `--out-dir` is specified only against the default emitting mode, but both commands route six other mutually-exclusive modes that emit no prompts: on `tp review`, `--merge`, `--record`, `--resolve`/`--resolve-all`, `--verify`, `--report`, `--status`; on `tp audit`, `--merge`, `--record`, `--resolve`/`--resolve-all`, `--status`. The spec says nothing about `--out-dir` in any of them, and mode routing is a documented part of this command's architecture (internal/cli/review.go routes them, and `--output` is already a flag that is legal only in one mode — the exact precedent this release complains about in §4). Test 8 then declines to decide the one case it does raise: "passing both is either coherent or refused with a hint" accepts opposite implementations, so it constrains nothing and cannot fail.
suggestion: State the rule once for the whole matrix — `--out-dir` is meaningful only in the prompt-emitting mode and is a usage error (exit 2) with a hint in every other mode — and rewrite test 8 to assert that one outcome rather than a disjunction. A test whose pass condition is "either behaviour" is not a test.

finding: §4 and §6 cover `--out-dir` only on the two prompt-emitting invocations. Its behaviour in every other mode of the same two commands is undefined, and several of those modes emit no `prompts[]` at all — verified: `tp review <spec> --verify` returns an object with keys `error`/`code`/`hint` in this repo, and `--merge`/`--record`/`--status`/`--resolve`/`--report` produce non-prompt payloads. Silently ignoring the flag in those modes is the failure `spec/0.35.0.md` §8a warns about (a typo that cannot be separated from a failure); tp's existing `--output` guard sets the opposite precedent by exiting 2 with a hint.
suggestion: State one rule for the whole flag: `--out-dir` is valid only on the prompt-emitting invocation of `tp review`/`tp audit`, and exits 2 with a hint naming the conflicting mode otherwise. Add it as a §6 test; it also resolves test 8.

finding: §4 closes with "It is additive: without the flag the emitted JSON is unchanged." That is falsified by §2 and §3 of the same release, which add two clauses to every emitted role prompt — the prompt string is a field of that JSON, so the payload changes with or without the flag. Test 7 notices and patches the sentence into "byte-identical to the current output apart from the two new prompt clauses", which is not byte-identity and gives no way to decide what counts as one of "the two new clauses" when a future round rewords them.
suggestion: Scope the additivity claim to what is actually additive: `--out-dir` changes the payload's *shape* only when passed (one new field per prompt); §2 and §3 change prompt *text* unconditionally. Restate test 7 against the shape — without `--out-dir` the set of keys on every object in `prompts[]` is exactly `{role, category, prompt, output_path}` and no top-level key is added — which is checkable, unlike byte-identity-modulo-prose.

finding: §4's evidence is entirely operator-side — 'both cycles therefore piped the JSON into a script', 'the step most likely to be skipped or mis-written under time pressure'. Under tp run, the primary model, the driver already holds prompts[] in memory and spawns from it; it needs no files on disk, so --out-dir buys the primary path nothing. P1 is 'every decision optimizes for the AI agent', so a flag whose only beneficiary is the human on the fallback path needs to say that out loud — otherwise it reads as an agent-facing decision it is not, and SKILL.md ends up documenting a flag the primary path never uses, which is a permanent context cost on every agent that reads it.
suggestion: State in §4 which path --out-dir serves (the interactive subagent-per-unit fallback and third-party drivers, not the tp run driver) and why the flag beats the driver simply writing the files it already has. Then the flag's per-agent documentation cost can be judged against a stated benefit.

finding: Non-Goal 1's claim that "A prompt that can be written to a file is a precondition for sharding, which is why this ships first" does not survive inspection, and it is asserted reciprocally rather than argued: spec/0.41.0.md §5.3 states the mirror ("A prompt that can be written to a file is a precondition here, which is why that ships first"), so one unargued claim appears in two files and reads as corroborated. Sharding as spec/0.41.0.md §2 defines it — "a role whose checklist exceeds a threshold is emitted as several prompts over disjoint item sets" — is a change to the `prompts[]` array, which already carries N entries with `role` and `output_path` today and needs no file destination to carry N+k. Nothing in spec/0.41.0.md §2's "what must hold" clause (no item dropped, none judged twice, overlap attribution intact) touches where a prompt is written. spec/0.41.0.md states its real precondition in its own §1 and §2: `spec/0.40.0.md`'s measurement, which is what decides the split key.
suggestion: Either name the mechanism by which sharding cannot be expressed in the existing `prompts[]` payload — and then it is a genuine precondition and belongs in §4 as a stated requirement, not in a Non-Goal — or drop the precondition claim from both files and keep the honest ordering reason §1 already gives: this is the smallest item and its cost is paid by every following cycle.

finding: Non-Goal 4's stated reason — "A fence there would need a hook the interactive path does not install" — is wrong on both halves. spec/0.35.0.md §6.2's PreToolUse denial is not gated on being inside a run; the plugin's hooks fire in any session that loads the plugin, and §6.1/§6.2 make that explicit by designing the `SessionStart` hook around the `clear` matcher, which only exists in interactive sessions. And this repository already installs an interactive PreToolUse write-block today (CLAUDE.md's `block-native-tools.sh`), so "the interactive path does not install hooks" is contradicted by the environment the spec was written in. Non-Goal 4 reaches a defensible conclusion (no fence here) from a premise that is false, which is how the same false premise gets reused in §2.
suggestion: Restate Non-Goal 4 on the true reason: the plugin's PreToolUse matcher denies a fixed list of tp state paths and was never intended to fence source writes, and widening it to the whole working tree would break the ordinary edit path that the same session uses for implement units. That reason survives; "the interactive path does not install a hook" does not.

finding: Test 1 asserts a negative over an undefined set: 'a prompt for a non-role unit does not' contain the constraint. 'Non-role unit' appears nowhere else in the spec and is never enumerated. The candidates are not obvious -- `tp review --verify` emits a prompt, `--perspective documentation|testing|code-audit` emits a single prompt, `tp next --brief` emits a brief, and spec/0.35.0.md defines eight unit kinds of which two end in `-role`. I have to guess which emitters get the two clauses and which are forbidden them, and the guess is load-bearing: --perspective code-audit is precisely a unit that reads source and might mutate it, so excluding it as 'non-role' would omit the constraint from the unit most likely to need it.
suggestion: Enumerate the emitters in one list: which prompt generators MUST carry the clauses, which must not, and why. If the rule is 'every prompt that names a findings output_path', say that -- it is checkable and does not depend on the word 'role'.

finding: Test 1's discriminator 'a prompt for a non-role unit does not [contain the constraint]' names a category the spec never defines, and the obvious operationalisation is false. Verified against v0.35.1: every emitted prompt carries a `role` field — `tp review --perspective testing` emits one prompt with `role: "test-planner"`, so 'non-role' cannot mean 'has no role'. It may mean single-perspective modes, or `--verify`, or `--report`; `--perspective code-audit` is genuinely a review role by any reading. The negative half of the test — the half that makes it discriminating rather than tautological — is therefore unwritable.
suggestion: Enumerate the units in scope by their invocation, not by a category noun: e.g. 'the corpus role prompts emitted by `tp review <spec>` and `tp audit <spec>` carry the clauses; the `--perspective {documentation,testing,code-audit}` and `--verify` prompts do not' — or say the clauses are carried by all emitted prompts and drop the negative.

finding: Test 1's negative half — "a prompt for a non-role unit does not" contain the working-tree constraint — names a discriminator that does not exist on the surface this release changes. "Non-role unit" is a `tp run` unit-kind term from spec/0.35.0.md §3.3 (`implement`, `decompose`, `review-record`, `audit-fix`, …), and `tp review`/`tp audit` emit no prompt for any of those kinds — those units get their text from the runner template and `tp next --brief`. Every prompt these two commands actually emit carries a `role` key, including the single-prompt perspective modes (verified: `--perspective testing` emits one prompt with `role: test-planner` and an empty `output_path`). So the test is either unfalsifiable against this release's mechanism, or it implies the constraint must also be injected into artifacts owned by spec/0.35.0.md — which no section claims.
suggestion: Define the discriminator in terms of what tp emits. If the intent is "the constraint rides on the panel role prompts and not on the perspective prompts", say that and name the perspective modes. If the intent is that `implement` units must NOT get the constraint (they exist to modify the working tree), say so as prose in §2 and drop the test — it pins another release's artifact.

finding: Test 3 measures success as 'the file count equals the panel size and each name derives from its role', but two emitting modes have no panel and no role name to derive from: `--perspective documentation|testing|code-audit` produces one prompt (per `tp review --help`: 'single doc change plan prompt'), and --verify produces one verification prompt. Verified in the default path, `prompts[]` entries carry both `role` and `category` -- but a perspective prompt's identity is the perspective, not a corpus role. If --out-dir is accepted there (see the mode-interaction finding) I must invent the filename; if it is refused, the spec should say so.
suggestion: State the panel definition used by --out-dir -- 'one file per entry in prompts[], named from that entry's role field' is precise and covers every mode uniformly, provided every emitted entry has a role. If perspective/verify entries do not, say what they are named or refuse --out-dir there.

finding: Test 5 asserts 'the written paths appear on the machine-readable surface' without naming the field, the object it hangs off, or its value form. Verified against v0.35.1, `prompts[]` already carries `output_path`, which is the FINDINGS destination the unit must write to — so an implementer who reads test 5 as 'reuse output_path' produces a payload where one key means two different things, and a driver that spawns from it feeds the prompt file where the findings file was expected. The test as written passes for that implementation.
suggestion: Name the field and its scope explicitly, e.g. each `prompts[]` object gains `prompt_path`, present only when `--out-dir` is given, absent otherwise; and state whether it is repo-relative or absolute (see the cwd finding). Then test 5 asserts a named key rather than a surface.

finding: Test 6 accepts 'exits non-zero' where tp's contract is a five-value vocabulary a driver branches on (internal/cli/exitcodes.go: 1 validation, 2 usage, 3 file, 4 state), and tp run itself is specified as 0 vs 4 precisely so the orchestrator branches on the code rather than on the transcript. spec/0.35.0.md §8a already lists 'exit codes that cannot separate a typo from a failure' as a hazard an unattended driver amplifies. Under 'non-zero' a driver that hits an --out-dir destination failure cannot tell it from a spec-lint failure or a usage error without parsing prose or re-running — the exact round-trip tp exists to remove, and it happens on the path where no human is watching. Compounding it, failing the whole command over a destination problem discards prompts tp has already generated, so the retry re-pays the generation cost, which in the review phase includes re-running every registered workflow.checks command.
suggestion: Name the code in test 6: ExitFile (3) for a directory that cannot be created or written, ExitUsage (2) for a malformed --out-dir value, and assert it. State separately whether the emitted JSON still reaches stdout when only the destination failed — if it does not, say that the regeneration cost is accepted and why.

finding: Test 6 demands 'writes no partial set', but only discusses the case where the directory cannot be created -- the easy one, where nothing has been written yet. The hard case is a failure partway through the panel: role 3 of 4 fails on ENOSPC, EACCES, or a name collision, after roles 1 and 2 are already on disk. 'No partial set' then requires a mechanism the spec does not choose: pre-flight probe of the directory, write-all-to-temp-then-rename, or unlink-on-error cleanup -- and they differ observably (cleanup can delete a file a previous round wrote; rename cannot).
suggestion: State the mechanism, e.g. write every prompt to a temp file in the destination and rename only after all N succeed, and say explicitly whether files from a previous round in the same directory may be removed by a failed run (they must not be). Add the mid-panel failure to test 6, since the directory-creation case does not exercise the rollback at all.

finding: Test 6 requires `--out-dir` on an uncreatable path to exit 'non-zero'. tp pins exit codes precisely everywhere else (0/1/2/3/4, with a distinct file-error code — `review --record` on a missing file exits ExitFile), and 'non-zero' is the one form that cannot distinguish a usage error from an I/O error, which is precisely the separation `spec/0.35.0.md` §8a lists as a thing an unattended driver needs. A driver branching on the exit code cannot be written against this test.
suggestion: Pin the code. Suggested: exit 2 for a malformed/conflicting flag combination and the file-error code for a directory that exists but cannot be written, matching the existing `--record`-on-missing-file precedent.

finding: Test 6 requires an undirected 'exits non-zero' for an uncreatable --out-dir. tp's agent-facing contract is a specific exit code (0/1/2/3/4) plus a hint -- that taxonomy is the reason a driver can branch without reading prose, and `tp run` itself branches on 0 vs 4. 'Non-zero' lets me ship 1, 2 or 3 and pass the test, and the three mean different things to a caller: 2 is usage, and a file/path failure has its own code (ExitFile) already used by --record on a missing file.
suggestion: Name the exact code for each failure -- an uncreatable/unwritable directory is a file error, a mode conflict (test 8) is a usage error -- and name the surface the hint appears on (stderr `output.Notice` vs the JSON error object), so the test asserts a code rather than a sign.

finding: Test 6's second half, 'and writes no partial set', is not discriminating as specified. If the failure is detected before the first write (a pre-flight mkdir check — the natural implementation) then no partial set can exist under any implementation, and the assertion passes vacuously; the informative case is a failure that occurs partway through the sequence (per-file permission, ENOSPC, a role name that is not a legal path segment), which the spec's trigger condition ('a path that cannot be created') excludes. The spec also does not say whether the guarantee is a pre-flight check or an all-or-nothing write (temp dir + rename), and those two have different observable outcomes for the mid-sequence case.
suggestion: State the mechanism (pre-flight validation, or write-to-temp-then-rename) and give test 6 a trigger that can actually fail mid-sequence — e.g. a directory that becomes unwritable after the first file, or a two-role panel whose second role name is unwritable — so the 'no partial set' clause has something to refute.

finding: Test 8 accepts two opposite behaviours: passing --out-dir with --merge's --output is 'either coherent or refused with a hint, never silently one-of'. A test that passes under both outcomes cannot fail on the wrong one, so it defers the decision to implementation rather than making it. The AX cost is concrete: an agent reading the spec to learn whether it may combine the flags cannot, and pays a round-trip to the code or to a trial invocation to find out — which is the round-trip tp exists to remove.
suggestion: Pick one and write it: either the pair is coherent (prompts to --out-dir, merged output to --output, since the modes do not overlap) or it exits 2 with a hint. Then test 8 asserts that single outcome.

finding: Tests 3 and 4 require 'each name derives from its role', which is not a naming rule — `tester.md`, `tester.prompt.md`, `review-r1-tester.txt` and `review-r1-tester.prompt.md` all 'derive from' the role, and two engineers assert different filenames. Three consequences the spec does not resolve: (a) no round number in the name means round 2 silently overwrites round 1's prompts in the same `--out-dir`, and the spec never says whether that is intended; (b) tp already computes `prompts[].output_path` = `review-r1-<role>.ndjson`, which is the FINDINGS path — a prompt file named from the same template would collide semantically with it; (c) corpus role names are user-supplied filenames under `.tp/reviewers/`, so the spec should say what happens to a role name containing a path separator or `..` before it becomes a filename.
suggestion: Pin the template literally (e.g. `<out-dir>/review-r<N>-<role>.prompt.md` and `audit-r<N>-<role>.prompt.md`), state the overwrite policy for a pre-existing file, and state the sanitisation or rejection rule for a role name that is not a safe path segment.

finding: §6 reads as eight numbered tests, but tp's own structured-element extractor does not see it that way. Verified with `tp lint spec/0.36.0.md`: §6 is reported as six separate lists (line 94 #1-#1, 96 #1-#3, 99 #1-#5, 102 #1-#6, 104 #1-#7, 106 #1-#8), and §5's four non-goals as three lists. The multi-line continuation indentation splits them. This matters for testability specifically: §6 is the acceptance surface this spec will be decomposed against, `tp lint`'s 'verify each item maps to a task' hint operates on these fragments, and my own reviewer prompt received the tests as six disjoint list checks rather than one list of eight — so a per-item mapping to tasks or to review coverage is built on the wrong boundaries.
suggestion: Reflow §6 (and §5) so each numbered item is extracted as one item of one list — either single-line items or continuation lines indented consistently with what the extractor accepts — and re-run `tp lint` to confirm §6 reports as one list of 8.

finding: §3's argument rests on the claim that a findings file's 'partial state is already valid input to `--merge`'. I verified this is true today — `tp review --merge` on a file whose last line is truncated mid-object skips it with a warning and exits 0 with the two complete rows merged — but nothing in §6 tests it and nothing in the spec pins it as a contract. This release makes that tolerance load-bearing for every unit that dies mid-round; a later change that tightens `--merge` to reject malformed input would silently invalidate the whole §3 mechanism, and no test would catch it.
suggestion: Add a §6 test: `--merge` on an NDJSON file whose final line is a truncated JSON object merges the complete rows, exits 0, and reports the skipped line — pinning the behaviour §3 depends on.

finding: The zero-role case is unspecified. Per-spec role activation (v0.32.0) can deactivate roles -- the emitted payload has a top-level `skipped_roles` key -- so a spec whose panel resolves to zero roles with --out-dir has no stated behaviour: create the directory and write nothing at exit 0, or refuse. Test 3's 'file count equals the panel size' is trivially satisfied by 0==0, so the test does not force a decision either, and a driver that spawns from an empty directory silently runs a round with no reviewers -- the 'dropped role merges clean' hazard again.
suggestion: Say what an empty panel does under --out-dir (a refusal with a hint naming the deactivated roles is the useful one) and make it a test rather than leaving it to 0==0.

finding: §4's payoff is that 'a driver can spawn from them without parsing prose', but neither §4 nor §6 says whether `--out-dir` is resolved against the process cwd or the repo root, nor whether the reported paths are absolute or relative. That distinction is the difference between a driver working and not: under `tp run` the child process is spawned separately, and a relative path is only meaningful if the child's cwd matches the emitter's. Verified that the existing `prompts[].output_path` is emitted repo-relative, so 'follow the existing convention' would produce exactly the fragile form.
suggestion: State that `--out-dir` is resolved against the process cwd and that the reported prompt paths are absolute (or explicitly relative to a named anchor), and assert the form in test 5.

finding: Non-Goal 1 claims 'A prompt that can be written to a file is a precondition for sharding, which is why this ships first.' That precondition does not obviously hold: prompts[] already carries each role's prompt text on the machine-readable surface, so a sharding driver can already split and dispatch without any file ever touching disk. What sharding needs is a divisible checklist, which is 0.41.0's own work. Since this sentence is the stated reason the release is sequenced first, an unsupported version of it weakens the ordering argument §1 also leans on.
suggestion: Either drop the precondition claim and let §1's real argument stand on its own (smallest change, cost paid by every following cycle), or state the actual dependency 0.41.0 has on --out-dir rather than on file-writability in general.

finding: §3 sells partial state as a benefit — 'a findings file is append-only NDJSON whose partial state is already valid input to --merge' — and the release's whole effect is to make partial-but-valid findings files more common. The hazard on the other side of that trade (a truncated round merging clean and being counted as a complete one) is routed to spec/0.35.0.md §8a, but neither §3 nor §5 says so, while §5 fences three neighbouring concerns and cross-references 0.41.0, 0.42.0 §9 and 0.37.0 by name. An unowned interaction that the mechanism visibly increases is re-derived by a reviewer in every round it survives, and the round-trip cost of that re-derivation recurs for the life of the review loop; one cross-reference retires it permanently.
suggestion: Add a fourth clause to §3 or a fifth Non-Goal naming where 'a partial findings file must not count as a complete round' is answered (spec/0.35.0.md §8a, and 0.37.0 if the convergence arithmetic is what changes), so the interaction reads as owned rather than overlooked.

finding: Test 1 explicitly names both surfaces ('for both `tp review` and `tp audit`'); test 2, which asserts the second of the two new clauses, names neither ('The emitted role prompt instructs incremental append'). Tests 3 and 4 restore the pairing for `--out-dir`. The omission in test 2 reads as an oversight rather than a decision, and an implementation that adds the incremental-write clause to review prompts only would pass test 2 as written.
suggestion: Give test 2 the same scope wording as test 1, or state once at the head of §6 that every clause requirement applies to both commands.

finding: Test 6 requires `--out-dir` on an uncreatable path to exit "non-zero", against a documented and stable exit-code table (0 success, 1 validation, 2 usage, 3 file, 4 state) that agent drivers branch on. "Non-zero" admits 1, 2 and 3, and the case is genuinely ambiguous between usage (a bad flag value) and file (a directory that cannot be created) — which is exactly when an unnamed code gets chosen inconsistently between `tp review` and `tp audit`.
suggestion: Name the code. `3` (file) matches the existing treatment of an unreadable `--record` path, which spec/0.36.0.md's own project notes cite as `ExitFile`; whichever is chosen, state that `review` and `audit` use the same one.

finding: Test 6 requires that a failed `--out-dir` "writes no partial set", i.e. all-or-nothing across N prompt files, in the same spec whose §3 argues at length that a partial artifact is strictly better than none because "buffering saves nothing and risks everything". The two are reconcilable — a half-written prompt set misleads a driver into spawning a short panel, a half-written findings file does not — but the spec never draws the distinction, and it names no mechanism for the atomicity it requires (write to temporaries and rename, or pre-flight the directory before writing any file).
suggestion: Add one clause distinguishing the two artifacts (a prompt set is consumed as a set; a findings file is consumed row-wise) and name the mechanism that makes the set atomic, so the requirement is implementable rather than only assertable.

finding: Test 7 asks for output 'byte-identical to the current output apart from the two new prompt clauses'. As written there is no procedure I can execute: 'byte-identical apart from X' needs a stated normalisation (strip the two clauses from the new output, then compare?) and a named baseline ('current' = which released version -- v0.35.1 at the time of writing, but the comparison will be run later). Without both, the test is either impossible (the clauses change the bytes) or vacuous (any diff is blamed on the clauses).
suggestion: Name the baseline version explicitly and state the comparison: capture the v0.35.1 payload for a fixture spec, remove the two constants from the new prompts, and assert deep equality of the resulting JSON -- which also gives the constants from the normative-text finding a second use.

finding: Tests 1 and 2 are presence assertions over text the spec never fixes: 'contains the working-tree constraint and the copy-out recipe', 'instructs incremental append, and states the reason'. Both pass identically whether the clause is one line or three paragraphs, so the acceptance cannot discriminate on the one dimension this release is spending — size. This is the presence-vs-size gap that makes an added-bytes feature grow silently across later versions.
suggestion: Do not pin the wording in the spec (that is task acceptance and would be over-specification), but do pin a budget: state a byte cap for the two clauses combined and add a test asserting the emitted prompt grows by no more than that against the v0.35.1 baseline. A cap is the measurable form of the claim §1 is implicitly making.
